title: A service is capped by its cgroup CPU quota

problem.summary: One service has a CPU quota lower than the work it is being asked to do. Its threads are repeatedly made runnable and then held off the CPU by the scheduler until the quota refills. The distinctive consequence is counter-intuitive: because callers stall waiting on the throttled service, the WHOLE system does less work, so host CPU usage falls even though threads are waiting longer than ever.
symptoms: one service is slow, and its callers slow behind it
the host looks quiet - CPU usage falls rather than rises
requests still succeed, but latency is high and throughput drops
no new process appeared and nothing is competing for the machine

discriminators.signal: host CPU utilisation during the incident, computed from sched_switch on-CPU time
discriminators.this_problem: utilisation FALLS well below its own baseline - the system is doing less work, not more
discriminators.not_this_problem: utilisation rises (co-tenant contention, host saturation) or stays flat (healthy)
discriminators.evidence: MEASURED on 17 labelled runs across four families. Cgroup cap 0.114-0.365 against its own 0.451-0.507 baseline (n=4); co-tenant 0.619-0.681 (n=5); host saturation 0.991-0.998 (n=3); no-fault 0.462-0.531 (n=5). The automated overlap check reports a clean split. This is the ONLY family whose utilisation moves downward. See evidence/cpu_cluster_separation.json

discriminators.signal: presence of a process consuming CPU it did not consume in the baseline
discriminators.this_problem: there is none - nothing arrived to take the CPU
discriminators.not_this_problem: a newcomer took one or two cores (co-tenant) or several (host saturation)
discriminators.evidence: MEASURED: 0 of 4 cgroup-cap runs had any newcomer, against 5 of 5 co-tenant runs and 3 of 3 host-saturation runs. One of 5 no-fault runs showed a small newcomer at 0.296 cores, well under the 0.988 floor of the co-tenant runs. See evidence/cpu_cluster_separation.json

discriminators.signal: direction of on-CPU time across the process population
discriminators.this_problem: broad, simultaneous LOSS of CPU time across many unrelated processes, because callers stall behind the throttled one
discriminators.not_this_problem: on-CPU time is redistributed or added to, not withdrawn from everyone at once
discriminators.evidence: MEASURED on a labelled cgroup-cap run: node 1.120->0.243, python3 0.767->0.137, java 0.673->0.278, dockerd 0.452->0.088, traefik 0.232->0.052, app 0.204->0.033. Largest single loss 0.876 cores against 0.024-0.134 for no-fault and co-tenant runs. See evidence/cpu_cluster_separation.json

discriminators.signal: runqueue delay: time from sched_waking to the sched_switch that runs the thread
discriminators.this_problem: raised - measured 13.54x to 15.70x - while the host is doing LESS work. Waiting more while working less is the throttle signature
discriminators.not_this_problem: runqueue delay alone separates nothing: it is raised in every CPU-family fault and in healthy load bursts. Only its combination with falling utilisation is diagnostic
discriminators.evidence: MEASURED: cgroup cap 13.54-15.70x, host saturation 36.97-52.54x, co-tenant 7.12x, healthy burst 3.69x. Treating raised runqueue delay as evidence FOR this family caused both mild-intensity cap runs to be misdiagnosed as co-tenant contention. See docs/FINDINGS-phase1.md findings F1 and F2.

unverified_do_not_claim.claim: the process that loses the most CPU is the throttled service
unverified_do_not_claim.measurement: on a labelled cgroup-cap run the target was carts, which runs as `java` and lost 0.395 cores. The largest loser was `node` - the front-end, a victim - at 0.876 cores. The biggest loser is the busiest caller, not the capped service.
unverified_do_not_claim.consequence: this blueprint may conclude THAT a service is throttled, but not WHICH one, until cgroup-aware attribution exists. Naming a service from comm alone would be wrong roughly as often as right.
unverified_do_not_claim.agent_note: Which process lost the most CPU time. This identifies the largest victim of the stall, not its cause, so do not report it as the culprit.

unverified_do_not_claim.claim: cgroup throttling shows up as a raised runnable-wait share
unverified_do_not_claim.measurement: runnable_wait of the labelled culprit never exceeds 4% in ANY fault family across 93 runs, and was 2.6% for the cgroup-cap family. The share is diluted by ordinary idle waiting.
unverified_do_not_claim.consequence: use per-wakeup runqueue delay and on-CPU attribution instead. Do not reinstate without new evidence.
unverified_do_not_claim.agent_note: The share of wall time a service spends runnable. Measured across every labelled fault it never exceeds 4%, because idle time swamps it.

reproduction.system: Sock Shop or Train Ticket on Ubuntu 24.04, LTTng 2.15, Docker 27+, single GCP n2 VM with 12 vCPU
harness_only: The recipe sets the quota with `docker update --cpus`: 0.2 for aggressive, 0.5 for subtle. Note the API trap recorded in faults/README.md - `--cpus=0` is a silent no-op, so restoration must write the saved quota explicitly and be verified against /sys/fs/cgroup rather than docker inspect.

collection_order.why_these: MEASURED BASIS. sched_switch gives on-CPU time per process per CPU, which yields both host utilisation and the per-process gain or loss - the two facts that decide this verdict. sched_waking adds runqueue delay, which is corroboration rather than evidence, since it is raised in every neighbouring fault. No metrics are needed: cgroup throttling counters would confirm the mechanism but are not required to reach the verdict, and the falling-utilisation signal is measured to separate this family from all three neighbours on its own.

processing.step: stage the stored kernel trace for reading
processing.expect: a CTF directory the trace reader can open

processing.step: attribute on-CPU time per process, baseline window against incident window
processing.expect: host_utilisation falling between windows, no newcomer, broad per-process losses

processing.step: measure runqueue delay as corroboration only
processing.expect: per-process p95 runqueue delay raised while utilisation falls

processing.step: Combine into the verdict and its artifacts: the JSON verdict, the CPU breakdown chart, and a plain-English explanation
processing.expect: state that a CPU quota is throttling some service, why the host looks quiet, and that the service is NOT identified by this evidence

processing.step: State the recommended action alongside the diagnosis
processing.expect: inspect cgroup cpu.max and cpu.stat throttling counters for the services on the stalled path, and raise or remove the quota on the one that is throttling

outputs.contains: verdict, host utilisation both windows, per-process losses, runqueue corroboration, and an explicit statement that the throttled service is not identified
per-process cores baseline against incident, showing system-wide withdrawal with no newcomer
that a CPU quota is throttling some service, why the host looks quiet, and what evidence would name the service
inspect cgroup cpu.max and cpu.stat throttling counters for the services on the stalled path, and raise or remove the quota on the one that is throttling

verdict_when: host CPU utilisation during the incident falls materially below its own baseline
no process consumed CPU it was not already consuming
on-CPU time drops across many unrelated processes at once
runqueue delay is raised over the same window, so threads are waiting more while the system works less

rule_out.when: utilisation reaches the ceiling rather than falling - the host is exhausted, not idle
utilisation rises and a newcomer took one or two cores - something arrived to compete, rather than a quota holding work back
utilisation is flat rather than falling, and per-process losses stay within ordinary variation
a single component's socket-waiting syscall inflates by an order of magnitude while on-CPU time is otherwise unremarkable - the system is blocked on something external, not held off the CPU

decision.root_cause_is: a cgroup CPU quota set below the service's demand

evidence_from_literature.claim: A cgroup CPU limit manifests in kernel scheduling state as threads repeatedly held off the CPU, with requests stretching from milliseconds to seconds while the CPU becomes underused
evidence_from_literature.source: Gelle, Ezzati-Jivan & Dagenais, Combining Distributed and Kernel Tracing for Performance Analysis of Cloud Applications, Electronics 10(21):2610, 2021 - the paper's worked example is exactly a control-group limit
evidence_from_literature.validated_on: our 4 labelled cgroup-cap runs, which reproduce the reported underuse: host utilisation fell to 0.114-0.365 from a 0.451-0.507 baseline

taxonomy.note: Covers any case where an administrative quota, rather than competition, holds a service off the CPU. Authored from Docker cpu-quota runs; the deciding signal - the host doing less work while threads wait more - should hold for any quota mechanism.

apply_when: one service is slow and its callers slow behind it
the host looks quiet or quieter than usual
nothing new is running on the machine
do_not_apply_when: host CPU rose during the incident
a new or unexpected process is consuming CPU
the affected component is blocked on an external call rather than on the CPU
applicability.cheap_precheck: compare host CPU usage during the incident against the hour before: if it did not fall, this blueprint does not apply

capabilities_required.why: the stored kernel trace must be readable
the decisive signal: utilisation falling, no newcomer, broad per-process losses
corroboration: threads waiting more while the system works less

stopping_conditions.conclude: utilisation fell against its own baseline, no newcomer appeared, losses are broad, and runqueue delay is raised
stopping_conditions.stop_and_switch: utilisation rose with a newcomer -> cpu-contention-co-tenant; utilisation reached the ceiling -> host-cpu-saturation; utilisation flat -> healthy-baseline
stopping_conditions.stop_insufficient: sched_switch was not recorded, so utilisation cannot be computed -> request it and re-run. Do NOT decide from runqueue delay alone: doing so misdiagnosed both mild-intensity runs as co-tenant contention

adaptation_rules.if: the verdict fires but the throttled service must be named
adaptation_rules.then: this blueprint cannot name it from kernel comm alone - the biggest loser is the busiest victim. Request cgroup throttling counters for the services on the stalled path, which is one targeted question rather than broader collection

adaptation_rules.if: utilisation falls but runqueue delay is NOT raised
adaptation_rules.then: the system is simply idle - demand fell rather than being held back. Report reduced load, not throttling

adaptation_rules.if: utilisation falls and one component also shows a hugely inflated socket-waiting syscall
adaptation_rules.then: prefer the dependency-wait explanation: the system may be idle because it is blocked on something external, which produces the same drop in work done

preconditions: kernel scheduler events are collectable or already collected
the workload is run under a cgroup with a CPU quota

historical_effectiveness.note: 4 labelled runs at two intensities, separated from 13 runs of three neighbouring families with no overlap on the deciding signal. Sock Shop only; Train Ticket owed. Does not name the throttled service.

policies.collection_order_rule: Use evidence that already exists before enabling any new collection. Escalate a tier only when the cheaper tier leaves a candidate cause unresolved, and record why.

scope.restrict_to: the hosts and time window named in the intent

privacy: do not retain personally identifiable data

requires_approval: widening the host scope or time window

policies.autonomy_note: Level 2 = policy-controlled automation: select and execute low-risk plans inside the stated constraints.

evidence_sufficiency.if_below_floor: name the unresolved question, pick the ONE additional capability that would settle it, check it against the overhead budget, and request it.
evidence_sufficiency.report_when_stuck: if the floor is still not met after the allowed rounds, report the best-supported hypothesis, its confidence, and precisely what evidence is missing - never present a guess as a diagnosis

provenance.authored_by: measured from the CPU-cluster sweep, 17 labelled runs across four families
provenance.notes: Written together with host-cpu-saturation and the revised cpu-contention-co-tenant, because none of the three is separable on its own. Directly answers findings F1 and F2, where both subtle-intensity runs of this family were confidently misdiagnosed as co-tenant contention. Every threshold comes from evidence/cpu_cluster_separation.json. Known gaps: Sock Shop only, and the throttled service is not identified. v2 (2026-08-29): added measured scenarios from the two-application re-test. The same fault produces different signatures on a short call chain and on a wide fan-out system; both are recorded rather than averaged into one threshold, because the point of a blueprint is to tell someone what to expect and where to look, not to be one tuned number. v3: fault_type set to the ground-truth FAMILY name (svc_cpu_cap). This field becomes `covers:` in the generated skill, which the harness matches against the family, and the diagnosis scorer falls back to identity for unknown labels - so a family name satisfies both, while the agent's own fault vocabulary satisfies only the second.

scenarios.note: SCENARIOS record how this problem looks on different system shapes. They are measured, not assumed, and both pictures matter: a blueprint carrying only one application's numbers would mislead anyone running the other kind of system.

cases.scenario: Short call chain - requests pass through most services
cases.recognise_by: a handful of services, and the affected one sits on the path of most requests, so its callers stall behind it
cases.what_you_see: host CPU COLLAPSES to a quarter or two-thirds of its usual level while threads still wait longer for a CPU. Measured: utilisation fell to 0.25-0.73 of baseline, runqueue delay rose 13.5-29.2x.
cases.confidence: high - the signal is large and unambiguous
cases.measured_on: the first application, 4 labelled runs at two intensities

cases.scenario: Wide fan-out - dozens of independent services
cases.recognise_by: many services, and the affected one is on the path of only a small share of requests
cases.what_you_see: NOTHING at the host level. Measured across 4 labelled runs: utilisation ratio 0.995-1.008, no newcomer, biggest process loss 0.03-0.06 cores, runqueue delay 1.55-1.81x. The host keeps working on every other request, so one capped service is invisible in the aggregate.
cases.confidence: none from host-level kernel data - do not expect to find it there
cases.do_this_instead: go straight to per-cgroup evidence: cpu.stat nr_throttled and throttled_time for the services on the slow path, or per-container CPU. Host aggregates cannot answer this question on this kind of system, and looking harder at them wastes time.
